breakfast.name: Fufu and Soup
ingredients: Palaver sauce: greens, palm oil, fish, meat
instructions: Make fufu: boil water, add flour, stir until thick
Make palaver sauce with greens, palm oil, protein
Shape fufu into balls
Dip in sauce
breakfast.description: Cassava fufu with palaver sauce — Liberian breakfast.

breakfast.name: Rice Bread
instructions: Blend cooked rice with banana and sugar
Add baking powder
Pour into greased pan
Bake at 175°C 40 min

breakfast.name: Biscuits and Gravy (Liberian Style)
ingredients: Tomato sauce, onion, scotch bonnet pepper
instructions: Make simple flour biscuits or use store bread
Prepare the gravy: saute onion and scotch bonnet in oil
Add dried or smoked fish, tomatoes, salt
Simmer until a thick, savory sauce forms
Pour over biscuits or dip bread
The Liberian-American food connection: biscuits from African American culinary tradition
Liberia was founded by freed American slaves — American food traditions arrived with them
Biscuits and fish gravy is a Liberian-American hybrid breakfast
The scotch bonnet and smoked fish bring it firmly to West Africa
The American biscuit meets West African fish sauce — a culinary history in one bowl
breakfast.description: A breakfast that tells Liberia's founding story — American-style biscuits with West African smoked fish and scotch bonnet gravy. Liberia was founded by freed American slaves, and its food carries this dual heritage: American biscuit-making traditions fused with West African fish and pepper sauce.

breakfast.name: Kongoli (Fried Plantains with Egg)
instructions: Peel plantains, slice diagonally
Fry in palm oil until caramelized and golden on both sides
The ripe plantain's natural sugars caramelize in the hot palm oil
Fry eggs alongside in the same palm oil
The palm oil gives a distinctive orange color and earthy flavor
Serve together — the sweet plantain and savory egg are a morning contrast
Ripe fried plantain is the most beloved West African breakfast component
The caramelization of ripe plantain sugar in palm oil is a defining West African flavor
Kongoli (ripe fried plantain) appears under various names across West Africa
The palm oil cooking method is the most traditional Liberian approach
breakfast.description: West Africa's morning sweetness — ripe plantains fried in palm oil until caramelized, served alongside fried eggs. The plantain's natural sugars in hot palm oil create a caramelization that defines West African morning flavor. Palm oil gives an earthy, orange richness to everything it touches.

lunch.name: Jollof Rice
instructions: Brown chicken
Sauté onion, tomatoes, paste
Add rice and water
Cook covered until done

lunch.name: Palm Butter Soup
instructions: Extract cream from palm fruit
Cook chicken in cream
Add okra and dried fish
Simmer until thick
Serve with rice
lunch.description: Rich palm fruit soup — Liberia's beloved dish.

lunch.name: Gbeh-Gbeh (Liberian Stew)
instructions: Brown meat or fish briefly in palm oil
The palm oil colors the stew orange-red from the start
Saute onion, garlic, tomato paste
Add dried shrimp — this is the umami foundation of West African stews
Add scotch bonnet — whole for manageable heat, chopped for more
Add cassava leaves or greens
Simmer 35-40 minutes until everything is integrated
The stew should be rich, oily, and deeply savory
Serve over white rice
The palm oil-dried shrimp-scotch bonnet triangle is West African stew's foundation
lunch.description: Liberia's West African stew — chicken or fish braised in palm oil with tomatoes, dried shrimp for umami depth, and scotch bonnet heat. The palm oil-dried shrimp-scotch bonnet triangle is the foundation of West African stew cooking from Liberia to Nigeria. Served over white rice, the orange-red stew oil is the visual.

lunch.name: Foo Foo (Pounded Cassava)
ingredients: Palm butter soup or pepper soup for serving
instructions: Boil cassava until very soft and pliable — 20 minutes
Pound in a mortar with a heavy pestle
Add water gradually as you pound — developing a smooth, elastic dough
Pound until the cassava is completely smooth and sticky
No lumps are acceptable — this takes strength and patience
Divide into smooth balls or mounds
Serve with soup — dip and tear by hand
Foo foo is eaten without utensils — the hand is the utensil
Form a ball of foo foo, press your thumb into it to make a dent
Use that dent as a scoop for soup — this is the correct technique
Foo foo is Central and West Africa's staple starch in its Liberian form
lunch.description: Liberia's pounded cassava — boiled cassava beaten in a mortar until smooth and elastic, forming a sticky, dough-like ball. Eaten by hand: shape a ball, press your thumb in to create a scoop, use that to lift soup. No utensils. The pounding technique, the hand-eating method, and the soup-pairing are West African starch culture.

lunch.name: Country Chop (National Dish)
instructions: Country chop is Liberia's national dish — and it defies a single recipe
It means 'local food' — whatever is available, cooked Liberian style
The foundation is always palm oil, onion, tomato, pepper
Add whatever protein is available — goat, chicken, fish, dried fish
Add starchy vegetables: cassava, plantain, sweet potato
Add whatever greens are available
Simmer everything together until it's one unified stew
The beauty of country chop is its flexibility — poverty food made proud
Every Liberian cook makes it differently — no two country chops are identical
It represents Liberian resourcefulness and the richness of West African cooking
lunch.description: Liberia's national dish — a flexible everything-stew of palm oil, protein, starchy vegetables, and greens, defined more by technique than specific ingredients. 'Country chop' means local food cooked in the Liberian way. Its flexibility is its philosophy: use what exists, cook it with palm oil and pepper, make it delicious.

dinner.name: Dumboy and Pepper Soup
instructions: Boil and pound cassava into dumboy
Make pepper soup with fish/meat and scotch bonnet
Serve dumboy with soup
dinner.description: Pounded cassava with fiery pepper soup.

dinner.name: Check Rice (Liberian Fried Rice)
instructions: Sauté onion in palm oil
Add tomato paste and fish
Add rice, stir-fry
Season with Maggi and pepper
dinner.description: Fried rice with palm oil and smoked fish.

dinner.name: Potato Greens Soup
instructions: Sweet potato leaves are more nutritious than spinach — a Liberian staple green
Chop potato greens — roughly or finely
Brown meat in palm oil
Add onion, garlic, scotch bonnet
Add dried shrimp or fermented fish for depth
Add greens, water to make a soup
Simmer 30 minutes until greens are tender and soup is unified
The palm oil colors the soup orange and enriches it
Serve over rice
Potato greens soup is eaten at least 3 times a week in most Liberian homes
dinner.description: Liberia's weekly staple — sweet potato leaves (more nutritious than spinach) cooked in palm oil with dried shrimp and scotch bonnet into a rich, orange-tinted soup. Eaten 3+ times a week in most Liberian homes. The sweet potato leaf is Liberia's most important vegetable, and palm oil is its most important cooking fat.

dinner.name: Liberian Collard Greens
instructions: This dish reflects the African American influence on Liberian cuisine
Wash and chop collard greens
Cook smoked turkey or ham hock in water until tender
Add collards to the pot
Season with onion, garlic, salt, pepper, chili
Simmer 20 minutes until greens are tender but still green
Optional: a splash of vinegar for brightness
The American-style collard greens adapted in Liberia with West African heat
Liberian collard greens with smoked meat is the clearest visible culinary connection
Between Liberia and the American South — the dish traveled back across the Atlantic
dinner.description: The dish that crossed the Atlantic twice — American-style slow-cooked collard greens with smoked meat, seasoned with West African scotch bonnet. Freed American slaves brought collard greens culture to Liberia; the West African spicing transformed it. The smoked meat-collard combination reflects the unique Liberian-American culinary exchange.

dinner.name: Festival Rice (Jollof Rice Liberian)
instructions: Blend tomatoes, onion, scotch bonnet into a smooth paste
Fry the tomato paste in oil — it 'fries' the raw flavor out
This step (frying the tomato paste) is essential — 10+ minutes
Add stock and rice together
The rice absorbs the tomato-onion-pepper broth
Cook covered on low heat until rice is done
The bottom develops a slight crust — this is prized
The 'party rice' of Liberia — made at every celebration
Liberian jollof has more scotch bonnet than Nigerian versions
The tomato-fry step and the bottom crust are the West African jollof fundamentals
dinner.description: Liberia's celebration rice — long-grain rice cooked in a deeply fried tomato-scotch bonnet paste until each grain is orange-red and fragrant. The critical step is frying the tomato paste for 10+ minutes before adding rice. The bottom crust (like Persian tahdig) is prized. Liberian jollof runs hotter than Nigerian versions.

snacks.name: Kala (Rice Fritters)
instructions: Mix batter with mashed banana, rise 30 min
Fry spoonfuls until golden

snacks.name: Fried Boiled Peanuts
instructions: Boil peanuts in salted water 20 minutes
The shells soften, the peanuts inside become creamy
Drain and either eat as boiled, or fry briefly in oil
Frying after boiling creates a unique crispy-creamy texture
The outside crisps, the inside stays soft
Season generously with salt while hot
Boiled peanuts are a Liberia-USA shared food tradition
The Liberian American community carries the boiled peanut tradition
Simple, addictive, and requiring only peanuts and salt
Found at every roadside and market in Liberia
snacks.description: Liberia's roadside snack — peanuts boiled until their shells soften and the nuts inside become creamy, then optionally fried for a crispy-creamy texture. Another Liberian-American shared food tradition: boiled peanuts appear in both Liberia and the American South. Salt is the only other ingredient needed.

snacks.name: Baked Plantain Chips
instructions: Peel green plantains — they should be firm and starchy
Slice very thin on a mandoline or by hand
Toss with oil, salt, cayenne
Bake or fry until crispy
Green plantain chips are starchier and crunchier than potato chips
The palm oil gives them an earthy, golden flavor
Season while hot — the salt sticks
Cool on a rack — they crisp further as they cool
Plantain chips are consumed everywhere in West Africa
The green plantain chips are a completely different experience from ripe-plantain dishes
snacks.description: West Africa's crisps — green unripe plantains sliced thin and baked or fried until crispy, seasoned with salt and cayenne. Green plantain chips are starchier and more substantial than potato chips. The earthy, slightly sweet-starchy flavor is distinctly plantain. A universal West African street and market snack.

snacks.name: Peanut Balls (Kola)
instructions: Grind roasted peanuts coarsely — not a paste, just crumbled
Mix with sugar and just enough water to bind
Shape into balls by pressing firmly in wet hands
Optional: roll in sesame seeds
The mixture is dense and satisfying
Dry slightly in a low oven or air-dry
The compressed peanut ball is chewy, sweet, and intensely peanutty
Kola peanut balls are sold at every Liberian market
High protein, high calorie — a working snack
The simple peanut-sugar combination is found across West Africa under different names
snacks.description: Liberia's market energy ball — coarsely ground roasted peanuts compressed with palm sugar into dense, chewy balls. High protein, high calorie — a working snack sold at every market. The simple peanut-sugar compression is West Africa's portable energy food. Often rolled in sesame seeds for added nutrition.

desserts.name: Sweet Potato Pone
instructions: Mix all ingredients
Pour into greased pan
Bake at 175°C 60 min
desserts.description: Dense, sweet potato and coconut bake.

desserts.name: Pineapple Cake
instructions: Cream butter and sugar
Beat in eggs
Fold in flour and baking powder
Add pineapple pieces and pineapple juice
The pineapple provides moisture and tropical sweetness
Bake at 175°C until a toothpick comes out clean
Cool, optionally frost with cream cheese or fresh cream
The pineapple abundance in Liberia makes this a natural celebration cake
Pineapple cake appears at birthdays and community celebrations
The tropical fruit cake tradition in West Africa reflects the fruit abundance
desserts.description: Liberia's tropical celebration cake — pineapple-studded batter baked into a moist, fragrant cake perfumed with fresh pineapple juice. Liberia's warm climate produces excellent pineapples year-round. Pineapple cake appears at birthdays and community celebrations, the pineapple's acidity keeping the crumb moist.

desserts.name: Coconut Candy
ingredients: Sugar, palm sugar, or brown sugar
instructions: Combine grated coconut and sugar in a pan
Add minimal water to start
Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly
The sugar melts and coats the coconut — then the water evaporates
Continue cooking until the mixture becomes sticky and starts to crystallize
The coconut caramelizes slightly at the edges
Pour onto banana leaf or parchment — press flat
Cut into squares while warm — it hardens as it cools
Coconut candy is West Africa's traditional sweet
Found from Liberia to Nigeria under different names — the recipe barely varies
desserts.description: West Africa's coconut sweet — grated coconut cooked with sugar until the mixture dries and crystallizes into a chewy, toasted-coconut candy. Found from Liberia to Nigeria with barely any variation. The sugar-crystallization point (between sticky and set) is the critical moment. Pressed onto banana leaf and cut while warm.

desserts.name: Groundnut Soup
instructions: This is both a soup and a dessert context — sweet in the Liberian tradition
Fry onion, tomato, scotch bonnet in oil
Add peanut butter or ground peanuts dissolved in warm water
The peanut butter thickens and enriches
Add broth, dried shrimp, salt
Simmer until thick and unified — 20 minutes
The thick peanut soup is rich, nutty, and complex
Groundnut soup is central to Liberian cuisine — it crosses meal categories
Eaten at celebrations, often as part of a soup succession
The peanut's richness makes it feel like a dessert course in some contexts
desserts.description: Liberia's rich peanut soup — ground peanuts dissolved in broth with tomatoes, scotch bonnet, and dried shrimp into a thick, nutty, deeply satisfying stew-soup. Central to Liberian cuisine and eaten at celebrations. The peanut richness crosses the savory-sweet line, making it feel almost decadent.

drinks.name: Ginger Beer
instructions: Grate ginger, boil 10 min
Strain, add sugar and lemon
Chill

drinks.name: Palm Wine
instructions: Tap palm tree
Collect sap
Drink fresh the same day

drinks.name: Sobolo (Hibiscus Tea)
instructions: Bring water to a simmer
Add hibiscus flowers, ginger, cinnamon, orange peel
Simmer 5-10 minutes — the liquid turns deep crimson
The color is dramatic — almost blood red
Strain, sweeten with sugar to taste
Serve cold over ice or warm
The hibiscus gives a vivid, tart, cranberry-like flavor
Sobolo/zobo/sorrel is West Africa's most beloved non-alcoholic drink
Found under different names from Liberia to Nigeria to Jamaica
The deep crimson color, the tart hibiscus, and the ginger heat are the identity
drinks.description: West Africa's crimson drink — dried hibiscus flowers simmered with ginger and cinnamon until deep blood-red, sweetened and served cold. Known as sobolo in Liberia, zobo in Nigeria, sorrel in the Caribbean — the same drink followed the African diaspora around the world. The vivid color and tart hibiscus-ginger flavor are unmistakable.

drinks.name: Cane Juice (Sugar Cane)
instructions: Press fresh sugar cane through a mechanical press (market stalls have these)
Or: peel, pound, and squeeze by hand — labor-intensive
The juice is green-golden, sweet, slightly grassy
Add a piece of crushed ginger for heat
A squeeze of lemon brightens it
Drink immediately — it oxidizes and loses freshness
Cane juice is sold at markets and roadside — cheap, fresh, natural
The sugar cane cultivation in Liberia and across West Africa makes this widely available
The fresh sugar-grassy-ginger combination is specific to raw cane juice
Industrial sugar bears no resemblance to fresh squeezed cane
drinks.description: Liberia's market refresher — fresh sugar cane pressed into a green-golden, grassy-sweet juice, brightened with ginger and lemon. The difference between industrial sugar and raw cane juice is radical — fresh cane is grassy, floral, and complex. Market stall juice presses make this a daily drink across West Africa.
